fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some notes added (most probably by K. D. MacDonald?). See below for details.]

item.description: policeman.
root of bulrush. Stewed in water, then squeezed and given to cattle for diarrhoea.
short, stubby seaweed taken from rocks. Boiled and mixed with flour. Given to animals as a vitamin. [NOTES: ‘chirain’ corrected to ‘chìrein’.]
warble flies. [NOTES: corrected to ‘fiarsnan’.]
staggers affecting horses. [NOTES: corrected to ‘a’ bhoil’.]
bastard staggers. Took the form of severe coughing. [NOTES: corrected to ‘strincealair’.]

applied to swampy, boggy land. Horses had to be kept away from such land during the aforementioned diseases [i.e. a’ bhoill/a’ bhoil and stringealair/strincealair (q.v.)]. [NOTES: “a’” put in brackets.]
an ulcer on an animal’s stomach. [NOTES: corrected to ‘butag’.]
alum. Salt substance. Placed on a plate, saucer and used to cure the above ulcers [i.e. bùtag/butag (q.v.)]. This was done by touching the ulcer with this substance. [NOTES: corrected to ‘alm’.]
horse’s ankle.
fluke. [NOTES: corrected to ‘sglopan’.]
the swelling of the cud inside a cow’s mouth. [NOTES: ‘an’ put in brackets.]
a makeshift fire. Embers taken outside to build a fire in a byre, shed. [NOTES: ‘dreosaidh’ corrected to ‘dreòsaidh’ and note added above – dreòsadh.]
bung in a boat.
the eye in a lobster pot. [NOTES: ‘an t-’ put in brackets.]
the net which extended from the eye [in a lobster pot].
the equivalent of ‘adag chruaidh’. Part of a rainbow. Indicated bad weather. [NOTES: note added above ‘cùlainn’ – cuilean.]
if a lobster was caught on the top of a lobster pot, this was a sign of bad weather. [NOTES: ‘a mullach’ corrected to ‘am mullach’.]
if a hook caught the fish anywhere other than in the mouth, this was also considered as signifying bad weather. [NOTES: note added – gabhail (probably meant to be the catch-word).]
the roaring of the sea with a white foamy surface. Signified wind after rain.
a bit of wood used for taking the ears off corn, oats, etc. [NOTES: note added above ‘ainn’ in ‘froisainn’ – ein.]
taking the shell off barley. [NOTES: corrected to ‘spiuladh’.]
barley placed in a tub and beaten with a spade until the caulk came off.
two strands of barley used to tie a sheaf. [NOTES: ‘dubailte’ corrected to ‘dùbailte’.]
a sheaf.
a rope made from horse’s mane.
used for a hiding place. Especially used in the sense of straying cattle. “Chaidh a bhò sgairt a’ falaich orm.” [NOTES: corrected to ‘sgairt-a’-falaich’.]
wild garlic.
ladle.
a corn stack.
the bottom half of a hay/corn stack.
small ricks, smaller than ‘còcanan’. [NOTES: ‘an’ in ‘prabagan’ put in brackets and ‘còcanan’ corrected to ‘cocanan’.]
rectangular shaped net used for holding freshly cut seaweed. Grid pattern.
as in someone being related to you. [NOTES: corrected to ‘a furain’ and a note added – “Chan eil mi furain riu idir.”]
a heather rope.
the part of a dibble where you place your foot. [NOTES: corrected to ‘sgonnan’.]
similar to the above [i.e. sgònnan/sgonnan (q.v.)], but on a peat cutter.
the penultimate seat at the back of a boat.
one of the intestines used to make white pudding. [NOTES: corrected to ‘dòmhlan’.]
